an0389.user: Want a sanity check on my Meta numbers before I push more budget. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,800, gross margin 47%, CAC ₹392, ROAS sitting at 4.6, CTR 1.9%. 90-day repeat rate is around 11%. On the surface this looks like one of my best months — am I missing something non-obvious before I scale?
an0389.assistant:
Your acquisition is genuinely good — that's not the issue. First-order contribution is ₹1,800 × 47% − ₹392 = +₹454 per order, and a 4.6 ROAS confirms the front of the funnel is humming. If this were the whole story I'd tell you to scale tomorrow.

The number that should stop you is 11% repeat at 90 days. That means roughly 9 in 10 buyers never come back, so every rupee of profit has to be earned on the first order — there's no LTV tail compounding behind it. You're acquiring efficiently into a bucket with no bottom. Scaling spend now just pours more water into the same leak; your CAC will drift up as you push volume, and with no second order to amortise it, contribution per customer actually worsens.

Fix retention before you touch the budget. Pick the single highest-leverage repeat lever for your category — a WhatsApp reorder nudge timed to your replenishment cycle, or a first-to-second-order offer — and get that 11% moving. Caveat: 90-day repeat on a 30-day snapshot is a lagging read; pull the actual cohort curve by acquisition month so you know whether 11% is the floor or still maturing. But the direction is clear — retention is the constraint, not reach.

an0390.user: So my email is pushing serious volume — like 1.36 million impressions last month, about 17,700 clicks, CTR around 1.3%. But only 98 orders came out of it, conversion rate something like 0.55%, AOV ₹2,050. I'm on broad-match keywords to keep reach high. The traffic is there, so why aren't the sales following?
an0390.assistant:
The traffic is exactly the problem. 1.3% CTR is fine — people are clicking. But 0.55% conversion off 17,700 clicks tells you almost everyone who lands is browsing, not buying. That's not a creative or landing-page failure first; it's an intent failure.

Broad-match is the mechanism. You're casting wide to win impressions, so you're paying to pull in people who are curious about jewellery in general, not ready to buy yours. High reach, low intent — the funnel was poisoned at the top, and no amount of checkout polish saves a visitor who was never in market. The proving number is the gap between a healthy 1.3% click and a starved 0.55% purchase: that collapse is a quality-of-traffic signal.

The lever is to stop optimising for clicks and tighten for intent. Cut broad-match, move to phrase/exact on your actual buying queries, and build out a negative-keyword list to bleed off the browsers. You'll watch impressions and click volume fall — that's the point; you want fewer, hungrier visitors. One caveat: 98 orders is a thin base to draw a hard line on, so layer in by-query conversion before you kill terms wholesale — let the data name which keywords are tourists and which are buyers.

an0391.user: Quick one — why do my two dashboards completely disagree? Meta says my campaigns are running at 4.6 ROAS on ₹7.5L spend, but Shopify's last-click report says it's more like 1.6. Which number is the real one?
an0391.assistant:
Neither, and that's the actual answer. You're refereeing two dashboards that are built never to agree.

Meta's 4.6 is modelled — it counts 7-day-click and view-through conversions and gives itself generous credit post-iOS. Shopify last-click is the opposite bias: it hands the entire order to whatever the customer touched last, so anyone who saw your ad, then searched your brand and clicked through Google, shows up as ₹0 for Meta. One inflates, one undercounts. The truth sits somewhere in the middle, and no setting will make them reconcile — they're measuring different things.

So stop trying to pick a winner between them. Anchor on the one number neither can fudge: blended CAC = total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. On ₹7.5L, that's your real cost of acquiring a customer across everything, and you manage the whole account to it. If blended CAC sits comfortably under your contribution per order, you're winning regardless of what either ROAS claims.

Caveat: blended CAC mixes channels, so it won't tell you which campaign to cut — but it's the honest scoreboard for whether the spend overall is working. Per-campaign decisions you make with incrementality tests later, not by trusting platform ROAS as gospel.

an0392.user: My CAC jumped 22% versus last week and I'm honestly freaking out a bit. Something's clearly breaking — I'm about to rip up the whole Meta strategy, pause campaigns, rebuild the audiences, the works. This week I had 91 conversions. What would you change first?
an0392.assistant:
Change nothing this week. I know that's not what the panic wants to hear, but a 22% CAC swing on 91 conversions is noise, not a trend — that sample is small enough that a handful of orders landing a day later, or a couple of expensive clicks, moves the number that much on its own.

The real danger here isn't the CAC; it's the reaction. Founders who overhaul an account every time a single week wobbles end up whipsawing — you reset learning, the next week looks different for a totally unrelated reason, and you never let anything stabilise long enough to read it. You'd be manufacturing the instability you're afraid of.

So hold. A real signal is the same direction for 3-4 consecutive weeks, or a move big enough that it clearly can't be a sampling fluke — CAC up 40-50% and staying there, not one noisy print. Until you see that, leave the campaigns running and just watch.

If you want something to do with the nervous energy, pull the last 8 weeks of CAC into a single line and look at the band it normally bounces in. I'd bet this week is still inside it.

an0393.user: Why is my CAC up this week? It's 18% higher than last week on Meesho Ads and I'm thinking I need to redo the whole campaign setup. I had 89 conversions this week if that helps.
an0393.assistant:
Before you redo anything — that 18% is almost certainly just noise. On 89 conversions in a week, the number genuinely bounces this much from random variation alone. A few orders shifting between Sunday and Monday, or two pricier clicks, swings weekly CAC by double digits without anything actually being wrong.

Here's the trap you're about to walk into: rebuild the campaign now and you reset Meesho's learning, the following week reads differently for reasons that have nothing to do with your change, and you'll convince yourself the rebuild 'worked' or 'failed' off another noisy week. That's how accounts get churned to death by good intentions.

So don't touch it yet. What counts as a real shift is the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks running, or a jump too large to be sampling — not a single week at +18%. Give it that window first, then decide with evidence instead of nerves.

an0394.user: Running a blended Meta + Google mix on my haircare line. Three days in: ₹21K spent, 16 conversions. Is my CAC good? Should I scale this or kill it?
an0394.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't know yet, and neither can I. 16 conversions over 3 days is far too thin to compute a CAC you'd trust — any number off it is statistical noise dressed up as a verdict. Scale on it and you might be pouring money into a fluke good run; kill it and you might be murdering a winner that hadn't found its footing.

The threshold that earns a real read is roughly 100 conversions, or a 2-3 week window — whichever comes first. That's enough volume for the CAC to settle and for day-of-week and audience-learning effects to wash out.

So neither scale nor kill. Let it run to ~100 conversions on the current budget, then we look at contribution per order against CAC and make an actual decision. Right now there's nothing to diagnose.

an0395.user: Trying to read my Amazon funnel for the month and something feels off but I can't place it. 44,000 visits, 3,010 added to cart, 2,189 reached checkout, and 516 actually purchased. CTR's 1.4%. Where's the non-obvious problem here?
an0395.assistant:
Your acquisition and interest are healthy — that's why it feels strange. Add-to-cart is 3,010 of 44,000, about 7%, which is a perfectly good top of funnel. People are finding you and they want the product.

The leak is at the very last step. Of the 2,189 who reached checkout, only 516 bought — that's a 24% checkout-to-purchase rate, when a working checkout should land around 50-70%. So three out of four people who pulled out their wallet still walked away. That's not an ads problem or a desire problem; it's friction at the moment of payment. Usual culprits: a shipping cost that only appears at checkout, a forced account-creation step, or missing payment options — no UPI, no COD — on a page where Indian buyers expect both.

The one move: instrument that final step and watch real sessions drop off. Don't touch the ad spend — it's doing its job. Find what surprises or blocks people between 'reached checkout' and 'paid' and remove it. Caveat: 516 purchases is a solid enough base to trust the 24% as real, but the *cause* needs eyes on actual checkout behaviour, not a guess — set up the funnel events or session recording before you start changing the page.

an0396.user: I run a vertical SaaS for clinics and I'm bleeding on Amazon Ads. AOV's about ₹1,800, my margin's roughly 28%, CAC has crept up to ₹930, ROAS only 1.9 even though CTR is a healthy 2.5%. The clicks are coming. How do I get my CAC down?
an0396.assistant:
You're aiming at the wrong target. Lowering CAC won't save this, because CAC isn't the disease — the margin is. Run the contribution: ₹1,800 × 28% − ₹930 = ₹504 − ₹930 = −₹426 per order. You lose money on every sale, and no targeting tweak closes a ₹426 gap when gross margin is only ₹504 to begin with.

That 28% is the whole problem wearing a marketing costume. Even if you were a wizard and cut CAC by 20% to ₹744, you'd still be at −₹240 — still underwater. The ads aren't broken; a 2.5% CTR proves demand and creative are fine. You're selling a product whose unit economics can't carry any meaningful acquisition cost.

So the lever isn't in the ad account at all — it's COGS, pricing, or AOV. Either get margin from 28% toward something that can fund acquisition, or raise AOV with bundling/order minimums so each order carries more contribution. Until the gap between margin and CAC is positive, every channel you run will look 'broken' the same way. Caveat: confirm that 28% is true gross margin after all variable costs — if it's actually lower, the hole is deeper, and if there's hidden margin you're not counting, the picture improves. But fix the economics before you touch the targeting.

an0397.user: Why is my ROAS so low on WhatsApp broadcast? I'm spending ₹14L, ROAS is only 1.8 which feels terrible. AOV ₹1,700, margin 65%, CAC ₹962, 90-day repeat 40%, CTR 1.4%. I'm getting ready to cut this channel — is that the right call?

You're judging a genuinely healthy account by a vanity number that was never designed to account for margin or repeat.

The move is the opposite of cutting — this is a scaling candidate. Push more budget into it and watch contribution per order, not ROAS, as your guardrail; as long as it stays positive, more volume is more profit. Caveat: as you scale, CAC will drift up, so keep an eye on the day contribution approaches zero — that's your real ceiling, not the ROAS number that's been scaring you.

an0398.user: Looking for the non-obvious read here. No-code SaaS, running YouTube. ₹12L spend last month, AOV ₹1,400, gross margin 68%, CAC ₹747, ROAS 1.9, CTR 2.0%, and 90-day repeat is 26%. The 1.9 ROAS is making me nervous — feels like I should be pulling back. Should I?
an0398.assistant:
Your instinct to pull back is the trap, not the insight. ROAS 1.9 reads as weak only because ROAS pretends margin doesn't exist — and at 68% margin, it matters enormously. Contribution is ₹1,400 × 68% − ₹747 = ₹952 − ₹747 = +₹205 per order. You're profitable on order one, before any repeat value shows up.

And repeat does show up: 26% within 90 days for a SaaS is solid recurring behaviour, which stacks more contribution on top of that +₹205 at essentially zero acquisition cost. So the true value per customer is meaningfully higher than the snapshot suggests. The account looks mediocre through the ROAS lens and looks like a winner through the contribution lens — and contribution is the one that pays your bills.

Don't pull back. If anything this earns more budget. Manage to contribution per order as you scale and treat the point where it nears zero — not a sub-2 ROAS — as the line you don't cross. Caveat: 26% repeat off a single 30-day window is a lagging read; pull the cohort curve to confirm it holds before you lean hard into the scale.

an0399.user: Why is my CTR down? Google Search, it dropped 20% this week compared to last and I'm ready to overhaul the whole account — rewrite ads, redo keywords, everything. I had 93 conversions this week. What's going wrong?
an0399.assistant:

Rewrite the ads and redo the keywords now and you wipe out the account's existing performance data, the next week reads differently for reasons unrelated to your changes, and you've lost your baseline while convincing yourself you 'fixed' something. Leave it alone for now. A real signal is CTR sliding the same direction for 3-4 weeks straight, or a drop too sharp to be noise. One week at −20% is neither. Watch it; don't touch it.

an0401.user: Curious about the deeper read on my organic numbers. Snacks brand, last 30 days: AOV ₹2,600, gross margin 52%, CAC ₹731 on the SEO/content side, ROAS 3.6, CTR 1.4%, 90-day repeat 11%. On paper this looks strong — what's the thing I'm not seeing?

At 11%, you're essentially running a one-purchase business in a repeat-purchase category, and that +₹621 has to be the entire lifetime value because there's no second order behind it. The lever is retention, before you pour more into the top. Caveat: 11% on a single 30-day snapshot is lagging; pull the cohort curve to see whether repeat is genuinely this flat or still building. But for snacks, that number is the story, not the 3.6 ROAS.

an0402.user: Narrow question — which ROAS do I believe? On my haircare Amazon spend (₹14.5L this month, post-iOS) the platform says 4.5 ROAS but Shopify last-click shows 1.8. They're miles apart and I can't tell which dashboard is lying.

Shopify last-click does the reverse — it gives the full order to whatever the customer touched last, so every buyer who saw your ad and then came back via a brand search or direct visit shows as ₹0 for the channel.
